interviewQuestions.question: What's the actual difference between hexagonal architecture and Clean Architecture?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Practically, none that matters — they're the same idea drawn by two different people. Alistair Cockburn's hexagonal architecture (also called ports and adapters) draws a hexagon with faces for each port; Robert C. Martin's Clean Architecture draws concentric circles with named rings — entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks and drivers. Jeffrey Palermo's Onion Architecture is a third variant of the same shape.

What all three actually assert is identical: a core with **zero outward dependencies**, surrounded by infrastructure that the core knows nothing about, connected through interfaces the core owns. Clean Architecture is more prescriptive about naming — it tells you to call things entities and use cases specifically — while hexagonal just says "ports" and "adapters" and leaves the internal organization of the core up to you.

In interviews I don't get precious about which term I use — I'll say "hexagonal" or "Clean Architecture" depending on what the interviewer said first, and focus the answer on the actual mechanism: the Dependency Rule, that source-code dependencies point inward only, and that crossing the boundary at runtime is fine while crossing it at the import level in the wrong direction is the one thing being prevented.

**Testing:** whether you understand the underlying mechanism or have only memorized one vocabulary and get thrown by the other.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: In Clean Architecture, what's the role of a use case, and why isn't business validation logic put there directly?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A use case's job is orchestration only — it represents one thing an actor wants done (`PlaceOrder`, `CancelSubscription`) and its body reads like a short script: fetch something through a port, tell it to do the thing, save it through a port, maybe publish an event.

The reason validation and business rules live on the **entity** instead — `order.canBeCancelled()` rather than an `if` chain inside the use case — is that entities are the layer meant to hold enterprise-wide rules that would be true regardless of which specific workflow is calling them. An order's cancellation rule (say, "can't cancel after it's shipped") is true whether it's triggered by a customer support agent, an automated fraud check, or a batch job — so it shouldn't be duplicated inside every use case that might trigger a cancellation.

The practical payoff: use cases stay thin and easy to read, entities become the single source of truth for a rule, and testing the rule itself (`Order.cancel()` after shipping should raise) doesn't require constructing a use case, its ports, or any mocks at all — just the entity.

When I review a use case that's grown a large `if` block encoding a business rule, that's my signal the rule needs to move down into the entity it's actually about.

**Testing:** whether you know where business rules belong within the ring structure, not just that rings exist.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Use cases

interviewQuestions.question: When would you tell a team NOT to use hexagonal or Clean Architecture for a service they're about to build?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
When the service's actual logic is thin CRUD with no rule complex enough to be worth protecting from the framework. The tell I look for is a hypothetical use case whose entire body would be `repository.save(mapper.toEntity(request))` — no branching, no invariant, nothing an entity needs to enforce. Wrapping that in four rings, a repository interface, a mapper, and a use case class is pure ceremony: more files, more indirection, and zero payoff, because there's no complexity being isolated from the framework.

Concretely, I'd skip the full structure for: an internal admin tool with a handful of screens, a one-off data migration script, or an MVP where the team's actual risk is not knowing if the product will be used at all — in that case the cost of the wrong abstraction is higher than the cost of no abstraction, because you'll likely throw the code away before the abstraction ever pays for itself.

What I watch for on the other side is teams using "this is just a CRUD app" as a permanent excuse once real business rules — discounts, approval workflows, multi-step state machines — accumulate on top of what started thin. At that point the calculus flips, and I'd rather introduce the boundary a version late than never, even though retrofitting it costs more than building it in from day one.

**Testing:** whether you can right-size architecture to actual complexity instead of applying it as dogma either direction.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You're debugging a production incident and the on-call engineer says 'the use case layer is broken.' How does knowing this architecture help you narrow down where the actual bug is?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It gives me a map of what each ring is and isn't responsible for, so I can ask more precise questions before touching code. "The use case is broken" is too vague — a use case only orchestrates, so the bug is one of a small number of things: a wrong sequence of calls, a port returning something unexpected, or an adapter behind that port misbehaving.

My first question is whether the *rule* is wrong or the *plumbing* is wrong. If `CancelSubscription` cancelled a subscription that should have been protected, I go straight to the entity — `Subscription.cancel()` — because business rules live there, not in the use case, and the use case itself has almost nothing to get wrong logically. If instead the subscription was never actually persisted, the bug is almost certainly in the adapter behind the repository port — a transaction that isn't committing, a retry swallowing an exception — not in the use case that called `save()` correctly.

This separation also tells me where to look for a *fix* without side effects: changing the entity's rule affects every use case that touches that entity, while changing one adapter affects only that one integration. In an incident, that distinction is the difference between a scoped fix and an accidental regression somewhere else in the system.

**Testing:** whether you can use the architecture as a diagnostic tool in a live incident, not just describe it in the abstract.
